input:
The performance of a mechanical-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was recorded over a period of one summer month, and the results give a picture of how the tower behaved under summer conditions. During the month in question, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 6 K, and the range was 5 K. From these figures it is possible to work out the actual water temperatures involved: the approach means that the cold water left the tower at 33 °C, and the range means that the hot water entered it at 38 °C.

To understand these terms properly, it should be explained that the wet-bulb temperature represents the lowest temperature to which the water could theoretically be cooled, and the approach is the difference between the cold-water temperature and this limiting value. The range, on the other hand, is simply the drop in temperature that the water undergoes as it passes through the tower. Putting the figures together, the tower was taking in water at 38 °C and returning it at 33 °C, against a wet-bulb temperature of 27 °C.

It must be emphasised, however, that these measurements cover one summer month and nothing more. How the tower performs at other times of year was not measured, and this is a real limitation, because in winter the wet-bulb temperature is much lower and there is no guarantee that the tower would hold the same approach or the same range. The results should therefore be treated as a description of the tower's summer behaviour at this particular site, and not as a general statement about its performance throughout the year.
target:
Over one summer month at a chemical site, a mechanical-draft tower ran with a mean wet-bulb temperature of 27 °C, an approach of 6 K and a range of 5 K. The approach places the cold-water temperature at 33 °C, and the range places the hot-water temperature at 38 °C. The three figures are means and differences over the month, and they carry the month with them.

The wet-bulb temperature is the floor for the cold water: a tower cools toward the wet-bulb temperature and does not reach it, and the approach is the distance the cold water stands above that floor. The range is the fall in temperature the water makes across the tower, from the hot water entering to the cold water leaving. The approach is the figure the tower is judged by, because it measures the tower against the limit the air imposes rather than against its own inlet state. Read together, the figures fix the tower's working point for the logged month: water entered at 38 °C, left at 33 °C, and the wet bulb stood at 27 °C.

The record is a single summer month. Performance outside the logged month was not measured, and the gap stands where it matters most: at winter wet-bulb temperatures the floor falls, the approach a tower holds against a lower floor is a separate question, and neither the approach nor the range logged in summer can be carried into winter. A winter figure would have to be measured in winter, on the same tower. The figures describe the tower as it ran in one summer month at one chemical site, and the claim for them ends there. Nothing in the record speaks for the tower in any other month, and the record is not extended by argument.
